## ❓Challenge questions

Use what you’ve learned this week to complete the following questions. Remember to use the script editor and to save your code as a `.R` script.


#### Question 1:

Create a numeric vector of at least 10 values representing measurements (e.g. weights of mice).\
1. Calculate the mean, median, and standard deviation.\
2. Use logical operators to identify which values are greater than the mean.\
3. Plot a basic histogram of your values using `hist()`.

```{r, echo = T}
mouse_weight_g <- c(50, 42, 33, 55, 39, 31, 44, 22, 41, 32)

#1. mean, median, standard deviation
mean_mouse_weight <- mean(mouse_weight_g)
median_mouse_weight <- median(mouse_weight_g)
sd_mouse_weight <- sd(mouse_weight_g)

mean_mouse_weight
median_mouse_weight
sd_mouse_weight

#2. Use logical operators.
# Recall the logical operators in R are:
## greater than >, less than <,
## greater than or equal to >=, less than or equal to >=
## equal to ==, not equal to !=

# Returns TRUE if the individual mouse weight is greater than the mean
mouse_weight_g > mean_mouse_weight

# If you want the values themselves
mouse_weight_g[mouse_weight_g > mean_mouse_weight]


#3. histogram
hist(mouse_weight_g)
```

#### Question 2:

1.  Create a new tibble with at least 6 rows of your own made-up data (e.g. plant growth under different watering treatments).
2.  Add a new calculated column of your choosing. Remember you need to assign the new output to an object name!
3.  View the new tibble by clicking on it in the environment viewer.


``` r
# 1. New tibble
plant_growth <- tibble(
  treatment = c("drought", "drought", "flood", "flood", "normal", "normal"),
  height_cm = c(16, 14, 18, 19, 25, 28),
  flowers_n = c(33, 36, 21, 23, 35, 34)
)

# 2. Add a new calculated colum
# (here I calculated a flower-number-to-height ratio)
plant_growth <- plant_growth |>
  mutate(ratio = flowers_n / height_cm)

# 3. View the tibble
View(tibble)

```

#### Question 3:

Make a tibble recording the heights and sexes of 8 imaginary plants.\
1. Add a new column that converts height from cm to m using `mutate()`.\
2. Use `group_by()` and `summarise()` to calculate the mean height for each sex.\

```r
# 1. New tibble (I copied and modified the one from Q2)
plant_sexes <- tibble(
  sex = c("male", "male", "male", "male", "female", "female", "female", "female"),
  height_cm = c(16, 14, 18, 19, 25, 28, 33, 22),
)

# 2. Calculate mean height for each sex
plant_sexes |>
  group_by(sex) |>
  summarise(mean_height_cm = mean(height_cm))
```

#### Question 4:

1.  Create a tibble of 12 students with columns for `name` and `favourite_colour`.\
2.  Use `count()` to tally how many students chose each colour.\
3.  Which colour was most popular?


```r
# 1. A tibble of 12 students with name and favourite_colour
# Note: you can continue on new lines when inputting data

favourite_colours <- tibble(
  name = c("Charlotte", "Louise", "Al Khansa", "Jessica",
           "Rana", "Deniz", "Magdalena", "Rebecca",
           "Ernesto", "Sophie", "Riannah", "Rosie",
           "Christine", "Zahraa", "Taoran", "Jake"),
  favourite_colour = c("Red", "Blue", "Green", "Yellow",
             "Red", "Blue", "Blue", "Yellow",
             "Red", "Blue", "Green", "Blue",
             "Red", "Blue", "Green", "Yellow")
             )
# 2. Use `count()` to tally how many students chose each colour
favourite_colours |> count(favourite_colour)

# 3. In this case, it was Blue (n = 6)
```

#### Question 5:

Work with a built-in example dataset, Edgar Anderson's Iris Data, `iris`, which gives the measurements in centimeters of the variables sepal length and width and petal length and width, respectively, for 50 flowers from each of 3 species of iris. The species are Iris setosa, versicolor, and virginica.

1. Load the dataset `iris` with `as_tibble(iris)`. Don't forget to assign it a name using the assignment operator `<-`.\
2. Inspect the new dataset object you created.\
3. Use `select()` to retain only the columns `Sepal.Length`, `Petal.Length`, and `Species`.\

```r
# 1. Load the dataset `iris` with `as_tibble(iris)`
iris_df <- as_tibble(iris)

# 2. Inspect the new dataset (any one of several options)
View(iris_df)
iris_df
head(iris_df)

# 3. Use select to retain only `Sepal.Length`, `Petal.Length`, and `Species`

iris_df <- iris_df |>
    select(`Species`, `Sepal.Length`, `Petal.Length`)

head(iris_df) # Inspect iris_df to check it worked
```
